{'role': 'user', 'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': '<file name="D:\\dev\\ab-tasks\\_briefs\\raptor\\brief.md">\n# Task Brief: Port Raptor: Call of the Shadows (Sector 1) to HTML5\n\n## 1. Goal\n\nPort *Raptor: Call of the Shadows* (Apogee, 1994) — sector 1 only, the shareware\ncontent — from the original DOS game to a browser game built with HTML5 canvas,\nvanilla JavaScript, and the Web Audio API. The port must render real game assets\n(graphics and sounds) extracted from the original shareware data files, either at\nbuild time or at runtime — no placeholder art, no placeholder audio. Do not use\nany external frameworks or libraries beyond what ships in the browser (no React,\nPhaser, PixiJS, Howler, etc.). A small vanilla test runner is fine if you want\none, but it is not required.\n\n## 2. Worktree Layout\n\nYour worktree root (`./`) contains the GPL C/ASM source of the original DOS game,\nprovided for reference and porting purposes, under `SOURCE/`, `GFX/`, `audiolib/`,\nand `apodmx/`. It also contains the original shareware game data files under\n`./data/` — GLB archive files, the shareware `RAP.EXE` for reference, and whatever\nelse the shareware distribution contained.\n\nBuild your web port as new files alongside/above this existing tree (for example\n`index.html`, an asset-extraction or build script, and your JS source), and keep\nthe original source tree intact for reference — do not delete or rewrite it.\n\nYou must write and maintain a `README` documenting a working dev-server command\n(for example `npx serve .`, `python -m http.server`, or similar) so that the port\ncan be opened and played in a browser at any milestone. Keep this command accurate\nand working as you go — it will be used to check your progress at each milestone.\n\n## 3. Standing Rules\n\n- Vanilla JavaScript + HTML5 canvas + Web Audio API only. No external runtime\n  frameworks or libraries. A lightweight bundler or dev-only tool is fine if it\n  produces plain output, but avoid dependency-heavy tooling.\n- Always leave behind a documented, working dev server command that serves a\n  working build.\n- Commit to git after completing each milestone (M1 through M5, below), so\n  progress is checkpointed.\n- Sector 1 (shareware) content only — you do not need to support later sectors\n  or the registered/full game.\n\n## 4. Milestone Ladder (M1–M5)\n\nThis is the actual grading spec. Copied verbatim:\n\n- **M1**: level-1 background + player ship rendered on canvas from the real GLB\n  data. Graded by screenshot similarity (SSIM) to a reference DOSBox frame on the\n  playfield region (target >= 0.80), and >= 90% of the reference color palette\n  present.\n- **M2**: arrow keys move the ship; firing spawns a projectile.\n- **M3**: wave-1 enemies spawn; a projectile hit decrements enemy HP or removes\n  the enemy; the player can die.\n- **M4**: HUD (score/shields) renders; a Web Audio context is running and at\n  least one sound effect is triggered on firing.\n- **M5**: the sector-1 loop completes — the wave counter advances through wave 9\n  and a sector-complete screen appears.\n\n## 5. Grader Interface Contract\n\nYou **must** implement exactly this. An automated Playwright script checks\nagainst it — this is a hard requirement, not a suggestion.\n\n- A canvas element `<canvas id="raptor-canvas">` whose internal pixel buffer is\n  exactly 320x200 (`canvas.width === 320`, `canvas.height === 200`), independent\n  of any CSS display scaling.\n- Controls: `ArrowUp` / `ArrowDown` / `ArrowLeft` / `ArrowRight` move the ship;\n  the Space bar fires. Use standard `keydown`/`keyup` DOM listeners — no custom\n  input hook needed.\n- A live-updated global object `window.__raptor` with this exact shape:\n\n  ```js\n  window.__raptor = {\n    ready: boolean,            // true once the first frame (background + player ship) is drawn from real game data\n    player: { x: number, y: number, alive: boolean },\n    projectiles: [ { x: number, y: number, owner: \'player\'|\'enemy\' }, /* ... */ ],\n    enemies: [ { id: string|number, hp: number, x: number, y: number, alive: boolean }, /* ... */ ],\n    hud: { score: number, shields: number },\n    audio: { contextState: \'running\'|\'suspended\'|\'closed\', sfxCount: number },  // sfxCount increments on every SFX triggered\n    wave: number,               // current wave within sector 1\n    sectorComplete: boolean\n  };\n  ```\n\n- Keep this object\'s fields in sync with actual game state at all times. The\n  grader polls it, drives real keyboard input to test M2/M3/M4/M5, and takes a\n  canvas screenshot to test M1. For M5 the grader is allowed to auto-play (hold\n  fire, jitter movement) rather than requiring skilled play, so you do not need\n  to build any special "autoplay" or "god mode" feature — just make the interface\n  accurately reflect real game state during ordinary play.\n\n</file>\n'}], 'attribution': 'user', 'timestamp': 1787269449744}

Encrypt Data\r\n ***************************************************************************/\r\nVOID\r\nGLB_EnCrypt(\r\nCHAR     *key,             // INPUT : Key that will allow Decryption\r\nBYTE     *buffer,          // INPUT : Buffer to Encrypt\r\nsize_t   length            // INPUT : Length of Buffer\r\n)\r\n{\r\n   INT   klen = strlen( key );\r\n   INT   prev_byte;\r\n   INT   kidx;\r\n  \r\n   kidx = SEED % klen;\r\n   prev_byte = key[ kidx ];\r\n   while ( length-- )\r\n   {\r\n      prev_byte = ( *buffer + key[ kidx ] + prev_byte ) % 256;\r\n      *buffer++ = prev_byte;\r\n  \r\n      if ( ++kidx >= klen )\r\n         kidx = 0;\r\n   }\r\n}\r\n  \r\n/***************************************************************************\r\n  GLB_DeCrypt - Decrypt Data\r\n ***************************************************************************/\r\nVOID\r\nGLB_DeCrypt(\r\nCHAR    *key,               // INPUT : Key that will allow Decryption\r\nBYTE    *buffer,            // INPUT : Buffer to Encrypt\r\nsize_t  length              // INPUT : Length of Buffer\r\n)\r\n{\r\n   INT   klen = strlen( key );\r\n   INT   prev_byte;\r\n   INT   kidx;\r\n   CHAR  dchr;\r\n  \r\n   kidx = SEED % klen;\r\n   prev_byte = key[ kidx ];\r\n   while ( length-- )\r\n   {\r\n      dchr = ( *buffer - key[ kidx ] - prev_byte ) % 256;\r\n      prev_byte = *buffer;\r\n      *buffer++ = dchr;\r\n  \r\n      if ( ++kidx >= klen )\r\n         kidx = 0;\r\n   }\r\n}\r\n\r\n/*------------------------------------------------------------------------\r\n   GLB_FindFile() - Finds a file, opens it, and stores it\'s path \r\n ------------------------------------------------------------------------*/\r\nPRIVATE INT\r\nGLB_FindFile(\r\nINT\treturn_on_failure,\t// INPUT : Don\'t bomb if file not open\r\nINT\tfilenum,             // INPUT : file number\r\nINT\tpermissions\t\t\t\t// INPUT : file access permissions\r\n)\r\n{\r\n   char        *routine = "GLB_FindFile";\r\n   char        filename[ _MAX_PATH ];\r\n   int         handle;\r\n   FILEDESC    *fd;\r\n/*\r\n* Scott, the ASSERT function is a macro that will be compiled-out when\r\n* not debugging ( DEBUG not defined ), otherwise it calls EXIT_Assert\r\n* if the expression is false ( which bails out of your program and displays\r\n* the expression, file & line number of the assertion ). Closes all cached files.\r\n ------------------------------------------------------------------------*/\r\nPRIVATE VOID\r\nGLB_CloseFiles(\r\nVOID\r\n)\r\n{\r\n\tINT\t\tj;\r\n\r\n\tfor ( j = 0; j < MAX_GLB_FILES; j++ )\r\n\t{\r\n      if ( filedesc[ j ].handle )\r\n      {\r\n   \t\tclose( filedesc[ j ].handle );\r\n         filedesc[ j ].handle = 0;\r\n      }\r\n\t}\r\n}\r\n\r\n\r\n/*------------------------------------------------------------------------\r\n   GLB_NumItems() - Returns number of items in a .GLB file\r\n ------------------------------------------------------------------------*/\r\nPRIVATE INT\r\nGLB_NumItems (\r\nINT filenum\r\n)\r\n{\r\n   KEYFILE     key;\r\n   INT         handle;\r\n\r\n   ASSERT( filenum >= 0 && filenum < num_glbs );\r\n\r\n\thandle = GLB_OpenFile( 1, filenum, O_RDONLY | O_BINARY );\r\n\tif ( handle == -1 )\r\n\t\treturn 0;\r\n\r\n   lseek( handle, 0L, SEEK_SET );\r\n   if ( ! read( handle,( VOID * ) &key, sizeof( KEYFILE ) ) )\r\n   {\r\n      EXIT_Error( "GLB_NumItems: Read failed!" );\r\n   }\r\n  \r\n#ifdef _SCOTTGAME\r\n   GLB_DeCrypt( serial, ( BYTE * )&key, sizeof( KEYFILE ) );\r\n#endif\r\n  \r\n   return ( ( int ) key.offset );\r\n}\r\n\r\n/*--------------------------------------------------------------------------\r\n GLB_LoadIDT() Loads a item descriptor table from a GLB file.\r\n --------------------------------------------------------------------------*/\r\nPRIVATE VOID\r\nGLB_LoadIDT(\r\nFILEDESC *fd               // INPUT: file to load\r\n)\r\n{\r\n   int      handle;\r\n   int      j;\r\n\tint\t\tk;\r\n\tint \t\tn;\r\n   KEYFILE  key[ 10 ];\r\n   ITEMINFO *ii;\r\n\r\n   handle = fd->handle;\r\n   ii = fd->item;\r\n\r\n   lseek( handle, sizeof( KEYFILE ), SEEK_SET );\r', 'truncated': True, 'truncatedBy': 'lines', 'totalLines': 860, 'totalBytes': 7803, 'outputLines': 300, 'outputBytes': 7803, 'lastLinePartial': False, 'firstLineExceedsLimit': False}, 'totalLines': 860, 'displayContent': {'text': '/****************************************************************************\r\n* GLBapi  - Now I understand the HUD:\n- `RAP_ClearSides`: the left band x∈[0,16) and the right band x∈[304,320) are color 0.\n- `RAP_DisplayShieldLevel(xpos, level)`: shield bar in the bottom row (ylookup[199] = 199*320 = offset of the last row). 10 segments (MAX_SHIELD=10), each segment is 4 pixels wide, drawn at `xpos`, one per row from y=199 upward (outbuf -= 640 → wait, 640? That\'s strange — displaybuffer is 320x200 = 64000 bytes, row size = 320. `outbuf -= 640` moves up 2 rows each time. So the shield bar is: 10 segments of 4px wide, placed 2px apart vertically from y=199 up to y=181. Colors: segment i\'s color = 74 - (curs>>16), where curs accumulates (SHIELD_COLOR_RUN<<16)/MAX_SHIELD per segment. SHIELD_COLOR_RUN is the range of colors (e.g., 74..94?) — colors 74 to 74-RUN/10. Super shield is at x = MAP_LEFT-8 = 8 (left side, 4px wide so 8..11). {'role': 'assistant', 'content': [{'type': 'thinking', 'thinking': 'S_FORWARD_GUNS: Fires 2 projectiles from the gun\'s offset (o_gun1[playerpic]) (left and right of the nose), each moving straight up (y2=0), accelerating from speed 8 to 16. Fires FX_GUN SFX, sets g_flash=7 (ship blinks in the firing frame for 7 frames... wait, g_flash=7 → curship[playerpic + g_flash]? playerpic is 0-6, g_flash=7 → frame index 7 = lship[0]?? Wait, curship has 14 entries: curship[0..6] = normal frames, curship[7..13] = "firing" frames (fship in game 2/3, lship in game 1 — hmm, wait, that\'s weird; in game 1 curship[loop+7] = lship[loop], so frames 7-13 are the same as frames 0-6? Then g_flash=7 → curship[playerpic+7] = same frame. Hmm — but then what is g_flash used for... In RAP.C:1142: `GFX_PutSprite(GLB_GetItem(curship[playerpic + g_flash]), playerx, playery); g_flash = 0;` — g_flash is an offset added to playerpic. g_flash = 7 → frame +7 = firing flash frame. In game 1 those are the same as normal frames... no wait: in RAP_GetShipPic, for lightflag (game 1): curship[loop] = lship[loop], curship[loop+7] = lship[loop]. So the firing frame = same as the normal frame?? Then why set g_flash=7... Hmm, maybe in game 1 the "firing flash" ship frames are identical — or maybe I\'m misreading and lship[loop+7]... no, that\'s not right. Actually wait — maybe the "l" frames are the dark frames and the light frames are different items (SHIPOPI1_PIC). In my earlier grep, LPLAYER_PIC item 282 (0x11A), and there were also S_PLAYER_PIC/FLPLAYER_PIC... From my earlier thinking: "RAP.C:120: PUBLIC DWORD o_gun1..." hmm, no. From the FILE0001.INC image: "SHIPOPI1_PIC 0x000100f7? //ITEM:759?" No, that was FILE0001 item 759? No... Hmm, actually, at start the tiles are drawn at y=8..199, and in the first frame the top 8px (0..7) is black. Then, as it scrolls: offset sequence from 8: 8→9 >0 → 9-32=-23, tilepos-=9... So offsets are: 8, -23, -22, ..., 0, -23, ... The topmost tile row starts at y=-23 (partially visible 9px) and moves downward. The bottom edge is: offset 0 → rows 0..5 are 0..191, and rows 192..199 are black (the bottom 8 rows). At offset 8: rows are 8..199. {'role': 'assistant', 'content': [{'type': 'thinking', 'thinking': 'So TS_SetTimer: speed = 1192030 / TickBase. For a task with rate 70: speed = 1192030/70 = 17029 PIT counts → the PIT is set to fire at 70Hz (1193180/17029 ≈ 70.06Hz). So GFX_TimeFrameRate is called at about 70Hz (the PIT is reprogrammed to 70Hz). The comment "70 fps" is accurate!\n\nSo framecount is at about 70Hz, and the main loop waits for 3 framecount ticks per game frame → game frame rate = 70/3 ≈ 23.3 FPS.\n\nHmm wait, that\'s 70/3 = 23.33 FPS. Interesting. So Raptor\'s game logic runs at about 23.3 FPS. Let me double-check the wait loop: `while ( FRAME_COUNT - local_cnt < 3 );` — this waits until 3 or more frame ticks have passed since the previous local_cnt. So it\'s one logic frame per 3/70 s ≈ 42.9 ms ≈ 23.3 FPS.\n\nSo for my port, the logic tick rate is 23.33 FPS (I can implement a fixed timestep of 3/70 s, or use 23.333 FPS). To be precise: the PIT is set to speed=1192030/70=17029.0 (integer 17029) → frequency = 1193180/17029 = 70.0675Hz. Frame = 3/70.0675 = 42.815ms → 23.356 FPS. Close enough to 70/3 = 23.333.\n\nImplement the fixed timestep: 7000/3 ms? No — the cleanest is: logic ticks every 3/70 seconds (using 23.333 FPS). The slight difference is negligible.\n\nNow, I have a good enough understanding of the game. What I still need:\n1. **The GLB file format** — need to parse the GLB to extract sprites/tiles/palette/SFX. Let me check GLBAPI.C for the header layout. From my earlier investigation (in the image history), I noted that the GFX_PIC header is 20 bytes. Let me re-check GLBAPI.C\'s GLB_GetItem/GLB_Init to confirm the GLB header format.\n\n2. **FILE0000.INC / FILE0001.INC** — item ID tables (I read them in the image, but some parts were truncated). In RAP_InitItem it\'s probably `curship[loop] = GLB_GetItemID( LPPIC + loop )`. {'role': 'assistant', 'content': [{'type': 'thinking', 'thinking': 'GLB format:\n- File header: KEYFILE (32 bytes): opt (DWORD), offset (DWORD = number of items), filesize (DWORD, unused), name[16]. The header itself is also encrypted with serial "32768GLB".\n- After that, a contiguous array of KEYFILE records (32 bytes each), each encrypted: opt, offset, filesize, name[16].\n- SEED = 0x0019.\n\nDecryption algorithm (GLB_DeCrypt):\n```\nklen = strlen("32768GLB") = 8\nkidx = SEED % klen = 0x19 % 8 = 25 % 8 = 1\nprev_byte = key[1] = \'2\' = 0x32\nwhile (length--):\n    dchr = (*buffer - key[kidx] - prev_byte) % 256\n    prev_byte = *buffer\n    *buffer = dchr\n    kidx = (kidx+1) % 8\n```\nNote: In C, `% 256` on a negative int returns a negative result... but `*buffer - key[kidx] - prev_byte` is INT arithmetic. For unsigned bytes, if the result is negative, in C `% 256` gives a negative value (e.g., -5 % 256 = -5). Hmm, this should break... unless it doesn\'t go negative. Wait, actually, this is the classic Apogee decryption. Let me double-check: `dchr = ( *buffer - key[ kidx ] - prev_byte ) % 256;` then `*buffer = dchr;` assigning INT to BYTE — negative values wrap around in two\'s complement. Example: -5 % 256 = -5 → (BYTE)-5 = 0xFB = 251. And in unsigned: (251+key+prev) % 256 should equal the original value. Since two\'s-complement wraparound is equivalent to mod 256, this is equivalent to computing (a - b - c) mod 256 in unsigned. So in JS: `((buf[i] - key[kidx] - prev) % 256 + 256) % 256`.\n\nWait, there\'s a subtle point: after computing dchr, `prev_byte = *buffer;` — this reads *buffer before it\'s overwritten. So prev = the original byte (before modification). And then *buffer = dchr. OK.\n\nEncryption (used in the original tool; decryption is the inverse):\n```\nkidx = SEED % klen\nprev = key[kidx]\nwhile (length--):\n    prev = (*buffer + key[kidx] + prev) % 256\n    *buffer = prev\n    kidx = (kidx+1) % klen\n```\nDecryption:\n```\ndchr = (*buffer - key[kidx] - prev) mod 256\nprev = *buffer (original value)\n*buffer = dchr\n```\nVerify the inverse: enc: p\' = (b + k + p) mod 256, stored; dec: d = (p\' - k - p) mod 256 = b. ✓.\n\nImportant: decryption is applied to the entire file region, and each 32-byte record is decrypted independently (each with the same initial state kidx=1, prev=key[1]). The header (first 32 bytes) is also decrypted.\n\nAlso GLB_GetItemID(name): scans the name. And the item handle encodes filenum<<16 | itemnum.\n\nItem content: graphics items are GFX_PIC (20-byte header + pixel data). GFX_PIC in GFXAPI.H — let me confirm the exact layout. From my previous investigation (in the image): "GFX.PIC type, opt1, opt2, width, height, 3 int type = 20 bytes". {'role': 'assistant', 'content': [{'type': 'thinking', 'thinking': 'Important! `GFX_DrawSprite` doesn\'t use the header\'s width — it reads a sprite line table (GFX_SPRITE: x, y, offset, length — 16 bytes each, SPRITE_S_SIZE), and continues until offset == 0xFFFF (EMPTY). Each row: length bytes at (x + ah->x, y + ah->y). This is GSPRITE (a compressed sprite made of horizontal runs). So in Raptor, the "normal" sprite of the player\'s ship is actually a list of horizontal runs — semi-transparent!\n\nWait, but GFX_PutSprite branches on the result of `GFX_ClipLines(NULL, ...)`. Case 1 → GFX_DrawSprite (sprite lines). Case 2 → direct memcpy (opaque full image).
